items.headline: Nvidia board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after reported Trump pressure; stock soars 31%, sparks broadest US rally since April 2025
items.summary: Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as President, CEO and a board director effective Nov 23, just 11 days after his abrupt Nov 12 resignation, saying it received input from senior US government officials and is confident he poses no national-security risk; reports say President Trump personally pressed the board over the weekend for Huang's return. Nvidia shares jumped as much as 31% (the most since 2003), helping drive the S&P 500 to +4.73% (best day since April 2025) and the Nasdaq Composite to +6.51%, snapping last week's correction.
items.actionable: The relief rally directly reverses the AI-capex-unwind shock that hammered the portfolio's gold/silver miners and HK tech last week, but a V-shaped tech recovery also reduces the macro case for Fed easing and could pull speculative flow back out of safe-haven metals even though GDX/SILJ/SLVP rallied alongside Monday's broad bounce rather than against it.

items.headline: Nvidia SEC accounting-practices probe remains open, unresolved by Huang's reinstatement
items.summary: Reuters/Bloomberg reported Nov 20 that SEC enforcement staff are examining Nvidia's accounting practices, including a 2025 change to how it reports revenue by customer geography; the report knocked roughly 13% off Nvidia shares that Friday and was the single biggest trigger of last week's broader market correction. The probe's scope and timing remain undisclosed and it continues in parallel with a separate DOJ antitrust review of Nvidia's Hugging Face acquisition.
items.actionable: This still-open accounting probe is the residual overhang behind Monday's relief rally -- any adverse SEC development could reignite the AI-capex-unwind selloff that hit the portfolio's miners and HK tech names last week, making it the single biggest tail risk to monitor this week regardless of Huang's reinstatement.

items.headline: Treasury Secretary Bessent warns Fed risks overtightening, breaking with hawkish Fed chorus
items.summary: On CBS's Face the Nation (Sun Nov 22), Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said 'many people believe' the Fed risks a policy mistake if it overtightens, citing already-substantial tightening in financial conditions and the fragility exposed by last week's rout. It's a high-profile dovish counter to recent hawkish Fed-governor commentary, and traders reportedly pared back odds of a 50bp December hike in response.
items.actionable: If Bessent's pushback gains traction and trims the odds of a larger December hike, it's a tentative positive for the levered silver/miners book, which was hit hardest by hawkish repricing the prior Friday -- but it is now directly contested by Williams's hawkish remarks the same week (see below).

items.headline: NY Fed's Williams says there's still 'work to do' on inflation, sees 2% goal only by 2028
items.summary: In a Nov 23 speech ('The Economic Mixdown') at the University of Mount Saint Vincent, New York Fed President John Williams said the Fed 'must take actions over time' to bring inflation back to 2%, forecasting overall inflation near 3.5% for 2026, slowing to just above 2% in 2027 and reaching the 2% goal only in 2028. He characterized the labor market and broader data as strong and not showing macroeconomic imbalances.
items.actionable: Williams's hawkish tone directly counterweights Bessent's dovish pushback from the same week, keeping the Dec 9 FOMC decision -- and Wednesday's Oct PCE print (the last major inflation read beforehand) -- the key swing factor for both the silver/miners book (real-rate channel) and the SGX bank/REIT exposure (financing costs).

items.headline: Gold and silver rebound sharply Monday as dollar rally pauses
items.summary: Spot gold climbed as much as 3.9% to around $3,678/oz and spot silver rose as much as 6% to roughly $43.78/oz on Monday, both rebounding from one-year-plus lows hit the prior Friday, as a pause in the dollar's rally and positioning ahead of this week's US inflation data drove buying. Last week's declines (gold -9%) had been driven by a hawkish rate outlook and forced liquidation to raise cash during the equity selloff.
items.actionable: Monday's bounce is the first real relief in both metals since the AI-rout liquidation began, but it was driven by a weaker dollar rather than a shift in Fed expectations -- a hopeful but fragile signal for the levered silver/miners book given Williams's hawkish remarks landed the very same day.

items.headline: COMEX silver vaults still historically tight (~101M oz registered) even as futures price whipsaws
items.summary: COMEX silver registered (immediately deliverable) inventory stood at roughly 101-102 million ounces as of Nov 19-20, out of ~331 million ounces total vault holdings, with eligible stock continuing to see net outflows. The structural Shanghai-COMEX premium (driven by the Shanghai Gold Exchange's 1:1 physical-backing/mandatory-delivery rules versus COMEX's largely paper-settled market) has kept a persistent double-digit-percentage premium in place through the year's volatility.
items.actionable: Vault-level tightness is a structural tailwind underneath the portfolio's silver/miner exposure independent of this week's Fed headlines -- a reminder that the physical-market squeeze thesis behind SLVP/SILJ/AG/HL hasn't been resolved by last week's paper-market selloff, even though it doesn't by itself guarantee a near-term price floor.

items.headline: China cuts margin ratio to 80%, floats ChiNext market-maker mechanism to stem rout
items.summary: Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges announced Nov 22 that the minimum margin requirement for buying shares on leverage will be cut to 80% from 100%, effective Nov 30, reversing a January tightening and freeing up an estimated ~RMB400bn. Shenzhen also opened a public consultation on a ChiNext market-maker mechanism (Shanghai did similarly for the STAR Market), alongside trading-fee waivers extended through 2028, all framed as support after the AI-led selloff hit Chinese tech names hard.
items.actionable: A targeted liquidity tailwind for HK-listed China tech (Tencent/SMIC/Xiaomi) heading into this week, though it addresses market plumbing rather than the underlying AI-capex overhang that actually drove the selloff -- a supportive but secondary factor next to Monday's Nvidia-driven sentiment shift.

items.headline: Taiwan widens short-sale ban to third round this month, NT$500bn stabilization fund actively buying
items.summary: Taiwan's FSC imposed a blanket ban (effective Nov 23) on short sales below the prior day's close and raised short-sale margin requirements to 150% from 130% -- the third round of curbs this month -- after the TAIEX suffered its worst weekly drop since 1991. The NT$500bn (~US$15bn) National Financial Stabilization Fund confirmed it has been actively buying shares since Nov 6.
items.actionable: Repeated state intervention in the Taiwan tech/semi complex is a sentiment floor for the correlated HK/China semis exposure (SMIC), but the scale and repetition of the stabilization effort itself signals how severe the underlying AI-supply-chain damage still is -- worth distinguishing policy support from an actual fundamental turn.

items.headline: Tencent Q3: profit -6% as AI capex surges, stock still soft into Monday's open
items.summary: Tencent's Nov 18 Q3 results showed revenue up 8% YoY to RMB207.3bn, but non-IFRS operating profit fell 6% YoY to RMB68.1bn as AI-related capex and new-product investment (Hunyuan, Yuanbao, WorkBuddy) weighed on margins; excluding the drag from new AI products, core operating profit was actually up 8% YoY with a 40% margin. The stock still traded weak into Monday, down about 1.7% to HK$338 amid broader AI-capex-fatigue sentiment and new US chip-export curbs on China.
items.actionable: The margin hit is self-inflicted AI investment rather than a core-demand problem, but it keeps 0700.HK sentiment tied to the same 'is AI capex paying off' question that whipsawed Nvidia -- expect the stock to keep trading on the broader AI-capex narrative rather than its own fundamentals this week.

items.headline: TSMC, Samsung suspend some China chip shipments under new US export-control rule
items.summary: TSMC and Samsung suspended some advanced-chip shipments to Chinese customers on Nov 19 while applying for licenses under a new US Commerce Department rule, effective the same day, that restricts advanced-computing exports to any data center worldwide providing more than 12 million aggregate TPP of compute to China-headquartered entities.
items.actionable: Tighter foreign-foundry access for Chinese AI customers is a structural tailwind for SMIC's role as China's domestic-substitution foundry (0981.HK), though SMIC remains capacity- and equipment-constrained and can't fully absorb diverted demand overnight -- a slow-burn positive rather than an immediate repricing catalyst.

items.headline: Singapore's STI posts worst week since April, breaches 5,000 then extends to 4,914 Monday
items.summary: The Straits Times Index fell 4.9% last week (worst since April) to 4,975.17 on Nov 20, breaching 5,000 for the first time in five months on imported AI-selloff and semiconductor-weakness fears, then extended losses Monday Nov 23 to 4,914.26 (-1.22%) with decliners outnumbering advancers roughly 3-to-1; DBS fell 1.26% to S$65.28 and REITs including CapitaLand Ascendas REIT also slipped.
items.actionable: The SGX banks/REITs/developers book (DBS, CityDev, UOL, Yanlord, HoBee, KeppelREIT, MapletreePACT) has been trading purely on imported AI-selloff sentiment rather than local fundamentals; Monday's extension of the slide into local hours despite Wall Street's Monday rebound suggests SGX needs a clean Tuesday follow-through on the Nvidia-driven rally before it actually stabilizes.

items.headline: Houthi strikes on Saudi refinery and Hormuz tankers coincide with oil sliding toward $90 on surplus fears
items.summary: Houthi forces claimed a Nov 22 strike on Saudi Arabia's Rabigh oil refinery and two more tankers were hit by projectiles off Oman on Nov 21, part of the worst month of Hormuz-area shipping attacks since the conflict began. Despite the attacks, Brent crude fell toward $90/bbl and WTI to around $83 on Monday as traders focused on a looming supply surplus ahead of the Nov 29 OPEC+ meeting, with returning Gulf barrels outweighing the geopolitical risk premium.
items.actionable: No direct energy holding, but falling oil despite active attacks on Gulf shipping is disinflationary at the margin -- a modest positive for the Fed's December decision and indirectly for the silver/miners and REIT book -- while the unresolved Hormuz risk is a latent tail-risk the portfolio's large cash pile should stay positioned to react to.

items.headline: Bitcoin crashes to ~$55k weekend low on $1.8bn liquidations, rebounds to $61-63k Monday
items.summary: Bitcoin fell to roughly $55,100-55,640 over the weekend on about $1.8bn of forced liquidations, then rebounded as much as 15% to touch $61,000-63,200 by Monday as the Nvidia-driven equity rally and a falling VIX eased risk-off pressure, with crypto liquidation volume dropping roughly 61% from the weekend peak.
items.actionable: No direct crypto holding, but Bitcoin's round trip is a clean real-time proxy for how fragile leveraged positioning remains across all risk assets -- the same forced-deleveraging dynamic that hit BTC over the weekend is the mechanism to watch for renewed stress in the levered silver trade if Monday's bounce fails to hold.

items.headline: Rare earth stocks rebound with the broader market; US-China rare-earth talks still in focus
items.summary: USA Rare Earth jumped 13% and MP Materials gained 6% on Monday as critical-minerals names rebounded alongside the broader market relief rally, with traders continuing to watch ongoing US-China talks over rare-earth export controls. Separately, Lynas Rare Earths heads into its Nov 25 AGM still without a permanent CEO after earlier takeover talks went nowhere.
items.actionable: Monday's bounce in MP is beta to the broader risk rally rather than a rare-earth-specific catalyst -- the still-unresolved US-China negotiating track remains the real swing factor for the MP/LYC.AX watchlist, while Lynas's leadership vacuum heading into Wednesday's AGM is a company-specific governance risk worth flagging separately.
